worksheet.title: Debug Detective
worksheet.subtitle: Find the bug, fix it, explain it
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find a bug in a longer program, fix it, and explain it.

parts.title: You are a debug detective
parts.text: This program is longer, and it has one bug. Run it, find the block that is wrong, fix it, and explain your fix. Then make your own buggy program for a partner to solve. The target is 4.

parts.title: Run it
parts.prompt: Run the program from 0, one block at a time. What number does Bit land on? Did it reach the target (4)?

parts.title: Find and fix the bug
parts.prompt: One block points the WRONG way. Circle it, swap it, and run again. What number does Bit land on now?

parts.title: You try — explain and create
parts.prompt: Explain why your fix worked. Then write your OWN short program with one bug, and the target, for a partner to solve.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A debug detective runs the code, finds the bug, fixes it, and checks again. You can find wrong, extra, missing, and out-of-order bugs — you are a debugger!

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: The unit finale: students debug a longer program (find the wrong-way block, fix it, explain why the fix works), then make their own buggy program for a partner. Find the bug, fix it, explain it — and make one of your own. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: tape a number line 0 to 5 on the floor and mark the target, so students can walk the buggy program and feel Bit miss.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20–25 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Run the mystery program one block at a time and watch where it goes wrong.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — it lands on 2, not 4; Exercise 2 — the wrong-way block is back 1; swap it.
3. Let them try. Students explain why the fix works, then make their own one-bug program for a partner (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — mystery program: 0, forward 2 → 2, back 1 → 1, forward 1 → 2. Bit lands on 2, not the target 4.
Exercise 2 — the wrong-way block is back 1; swap it to forward 1: 0 → 2 → 3 → 4. Bit reaches the target, 4.

Exercise 3 — explanation: the back 1 block moved Bit away from the target; forward 1 keeps Bit heading to 4. Make-your-own is open; a sample is start 0, forward 1, forward 1 with target 3 (a missing-block bug — add one more forward 1).

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: stopping after the fix without explaining why. Have them say what the wrong block did.
Make it easier: walk the mystery program on the floor line.
Make it harder: ask the partner to name the kind of bug before fixing it.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students follow (or write) step-by-step instructions, in order, to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a program, change a block to fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child fixes the mystery program, explains the fix, and writes a solvable one-bug program of their own.
